extracted.intended_audience: LaTeX users and package authors who want to create graphics with TikZ/pgf (beginners through advanced users; includes those who may port drivers or write frontends)
extracted.subtask_short: using TikZ and pgf for graphics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for creating graphics with the pgf/TikZ system: which layer to use (TikZ, basic, system), comparisons with alternative packages, useful utility packages, how to read the manual, and how to get help and report bugs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of TikZ (advantages and disadvantages)
rubrics_metrics.description: TikZ is a 'programming' approach to graphics that gives the advantages of the TeX approach: quick creation of simple graphics, precise positioning, use of macros, often superior typography. It is not a drawing program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh the trade-offs: advantages — quick creation of simple graphics, precise positioning, macro reuse, superior typography; disadvantages — steep learning curve, no WYSIWYG, small changes require long recompilation, code does not immediately show visual result. Use TikZ if you accept these tradeoffs; avoid it if you require interactive WYSIWYG editing or very fast visual iteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer selection — System layer
rubrics_metrics.description: The system layer 'provides a complete abstraction of what is going on "in the driver"' (driver = dvips, dvipdfm, pdftex). It is minimalistic and abstracts driver differences via low-level commands like \pgfsys@lineto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use the system layer directly as a normal user. Use the system layer only if you intend to port pgf to a new driver or write your own frontend; each additional system command increases porting work. Recognize that system-layer commands are low-level driver abstractions and are intentionally minimal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Layer selection — Basic layer
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic layer provides a set of basic commands that let you produce complex graphics more easily than using the system layer; it contains a core (several interdependent packages) and additional modules for special-purpose commands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the basic layer when you need finer control than TikZ exposes but want higher-level primitives than the system layer. Be aware that code for the basic layer can be verbose; use modules to get features (e.g., node management, plotting). The core must be loaded en bloc; load only the modules you need (e.g., beamer uses only the core).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the TikZ frontend for most users
rubrics_metrics.description: TikZ is a frontend that makes the basic layer easier to use; it reduces verbosity (example: \draw (0,0) -- (1,0) -- (1,1) -- cycle; instead of many basic-layer commands).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For almost all users, use TikZ rather than writing directly against the basic or system layers. TikZ exposes the full functionality of pgf but with a friendlier syntax (mixture of metafont and pstricks ideas). Only consider other frontends or the basic/system layers for special purposes (e.g., experimentation, frontend development, driver portability).

rubrics_metrics.name: Module and package loading discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic layer consists of a core plus additional modules. Some packages use only the core (e.g., beamer) and not other modules (e.g., shapes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Load only the modules you need to avoid unnecessary complexity. Understand which modules provide which features so that your document stays lean and portable. Recognize that some functionality is intentionally separated into modules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choosing a graphics package — portability vs power
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare TikZ/pgf with alternatives on axes such as portability, power, syntax consistency, and ease of labels.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard LaTeX {picture} environment for maximal portability but limited features. Use pstricks for very powerful graphics when PostScript output is acceptable (not portable to pdftex). Consider xypic if specialized features are needed but expect a steeper learning curve. Use metapost for powerful external-program graphics, noting label inclusion was historically harder (now integrated in LuaTeX). Use xfig if you prefer a GUI and convert to TikZ if needed. Choose based on whether you prioritize portability (pdftex compatibility), syntax consistency, or raw power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pgfkeys for key management
rubrics_metrics.description: The pgfkeys package defines a powerful key management facility and can be used independently of pgf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ pgfkeys to manage options and keys in your package or document code to keep interfaces consistent and flexible. Prefer pgfkeys over ad-hoc key handling for maintainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pgffor for loops and repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: The pgffor package defines a useful \foreach statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use \foreach from pgffor to repeat drawing patterns, iterate over coordinates or values, and keep drawing code concise and declarative rather than manually duplicating commands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pgfcalendar for calendar/date macros
rubrics_metrics.description: The pgfcalendar package defines macros for creating calendars; calendars can be rendered using pgf’s graphics engine or typeset using normal text. The package also defines commands for working with dates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pgfcalendar when your graphics or documents need calendar layouts or date computations; choose whether to render as graphics or text depending on styling and portability needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use pgfpages for page assembly and N-up printing
rubrics_metrics.description: The pgfpages package assembles several 'virtual pages' into a single physical page, allowing two-page-on-one-page versions, logos, watermarks, up to 16 pages per page, borders, and more.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pgfpages to create N-up prints, add watermarks/logos, or otherwise manipulate page shipout without external tools. The package intercepts shipout and arranges virtual pages into a physical page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommended reading order for the manual
rubrics_metrics.description: The manual is organized roughly by user-friendliness: easiest/frequently used commands and subpackages first; low-level and esoteric features later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not yet installed: read Installation first. Then read the Tutorial. Finally, skim through the TikZ description. Read the basic layer sections only if you need them; read the system layer only if you intend to write your own frontend or port pgf to a new driver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual notation and color conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public commands/environments provided by the system are printed in red; text shown in green is optional and can be left out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reading the manual, use the color conventions to identify public commands (red) and optional components (green) so you can quickly tell which arguments/options are mandatory vs optional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Getting help and bug-reporting etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: When you need help: (1) read the manual for the relevant part; (2) check the GitHub development page for existing reports/solutions; (3) use forums, mailing lists, and bug trackers; (4) before filing an installation bug, check the .log file to ensure right files are loaded; (5) email the authors as a last resort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the listed escalation path: manual → GitHub → forums/mailing list → bug report (with .log attached) → direct email. Especially for installation issues, include the .log output which shows file loading paths; this resolves most installation problems. Use the pgf mailing list to increase chances of response rather than emailing individual authors directly.
